question: What is the meaning of circularity in relation to circularity?
description: Circularity refers to the extent to which a product or material is designed and produced to be reused, recycled, or biodegradable, thereby minimizing waste and maximizing the use of resources. In the context of sustainable construction, circular economy principles aim to transform the built environment by promoting the reuse and recycling of materials, reducing waste, and preserving natural capital. Circularity is a key concept in the circular economy, as it enables resource efficiency and supports the longevity of products and materials.

references.text:
The circular economy is a system that enables resource efficiency by 
minimizing waste and maximizing the reuse and recycling of materials 
(Ellen MacArthur, 2013). It aims to eradicate waste and pollution, and 
support the longevity of products and materials, thereby preserving, 
restoring, and regenerating natural capital (Sch¨oggl et al., 2023). In the 
built environment, where the construction and operation of buildings 
account for a significant portion of global resource consumption and 
waste generation, transformation to the circular economy offers a 
promising solution to promote sustainable production and consumption 
as well as reduce the resulting environmental and societal impact 
(Calzolari et al., 2021). Circular economy, as depicted in Fig. 1, includes 
components such as circular business model (Ranta et al., 2018), circular 
design practices (Joensuu et al., 2020), and reverse logistics (Mallick 
et al., 2023) and it is supported by enables of circularity such as policies, 
standards, regulations, markets, consumer behavior, culture and tech­
nologies (Qazi and Appolloni, 2022). Among these enablers, the adop­

3.1.5
Temporal properties
Figure 7 shows the temporal property facet. The temporal properties play an essential
role in the life cycle management of products and materials.
Figure 7: Temporal properties facet of the MPO.
The TemporalProperty is used to describe time-related properties such as the Expect-
edLifetime and ServiceLife. The inclusion of these data helps to support estimates the
durability of products, and decisions about the timing, frequency, and method of mainte-
nance, repair, and replacement of materials, warranties, and replacement cycles.
3.1.6
Thermal properties
Figure 8 shows the thermal property facet. The ThermalProperty describes the thermal
characteristics of materials and products, including the HeatTransferCoefficient, Ther-
malConductivity, and SpecificHeat. These are critical in optimising product designs for
effective thermal management, insulation, and to meet regulations.
3.1.7
Chemical and biological properties
Figure 9 shows the chemical and biological property facet. These properties are essen-
tial for determining the appropriate end-of-life management of materials, including their
potential for energy recovery, composting, and disposal in landfills.
The ChemicalProperty is used to describe the Toxicity and Flammability of a of a product,
component, or material. The BiologicalProperty is used to represent Biodegradability.
Understanding toxicity and flammability is important for preventing environmental con-
tamination, while knowledge of biodegradability informs composting practices, thereby
reducing long-term environmental impact. For example, film adhesive and epoxy resin in
the crossbeam can be used for energy recovery, while PU foam may be directed to landfill.
